content:
Quick answer: A daily mobility routine means moving each joint gently through its comfortable range every day. For arthritis, a good plan is a 5-minute wake-up in bed, a 10-minute routine after breakfast, short movement breaks every 30 to 60 minutes, and a gentle evening wind-down. Move slowly, never force a stretch, and stop for sharp pain.

Stiff joints are one of the most common complaints in arthritis. Many people find they are stiffest first thing in the morning, after sitting for a while, or at the end of a busy day. A daily mobility routine is a simple, low-effort way to keep joints moving and reduce that stiffness. It does not replace strengthening or fitness exercise, which NICE recommends as core treatments for osteoarthritis, but it makes everything else easier. This guide gives you a whole-day plan, from a few movements in bed to an evening wind-down, with options for every ability.

What is mobility exercise?

Mobility exercises move a joint slowly and smoothly through its available range, without forcing it. They are slightly different from stretching:

TypeWhat it involvesMain purpose
Mobility (range of motion)Moving a joint repeatedly through a comfortable range, such as ankle circles or shoulder rollsEase stiffness, keep joints moving, lubricate joints
StretchingHolding a muscle in a lengthened position for 20 to 30 secondsImprove muscle flexibility
StrengtheningWorking muscles against resistanceSupport and protect joints
AerobicActivity that raises your heart rate, such as walking or cyclingFitness, weight, mood, general health

A balanced week includes all four. Mobility is the easiest to do every day and is often the first thing people notice a difference from.

Why daily mobility helps with arthritis

  • Eases stiffness. Movement helps joints feel looser, especially after rest.
  • Helps joint health. Joint cartilage depends on movement and loading to stay healthy.
  • Keeps everyday tasks possible. Reaching a high shelf, putting on socks, turning to reverse the car and getting in and out of the bath all need joint range.
  • Warms you up for other activity. A few minutes of mobility before a walk or strength session makes them more comfortable.
  • Breaks up sitting. UK guidelines advise breaking up long periods of sitting with light activity.

Golden rules

  • Move slowly and smoothly. Avoid bouncing or jerking.
  • Stay within a comfortable range. Mild stretch or tightness is fine; sharp pain is not.
  • Breathe normally throughout. Do not hold your breath.
  • Start with 5 repetitions of each movement and build up to 10.
  • Little and often works best: several short sessions are better than one long one.
  • Expect some movements to feel easier on some days than others. That is normal.

Part 1: 5-minute wake-up in bed

Do these lying on your back before you get up. They help ease morning stiffness and make getting out of bed easier.

  1. Deep breathing, 5 breaths. Breathe in slowly through your nose, letting your tummy rise, and out slowly through your mouth.
  2. Ankle pumps, 10. Point your toes away from you, then pull them back towards you.
  3. Ankle circles, 5 each way. Draw slow circles with your feet.
  4. Heel slides, 5 each leg. Slide one heel towards your bottom to bend your knee, then slide it back down.
  5. Knee rocking, 10. With both knees bent and feet flat on the bed, gently let your knees rock from side to side.
  6. Finger and wrist moves, 5 each. Open and close your hands, then bend your wrists up and down.
  7. Arm lifts, 5. Lift both arms up towards the ceiling and back over your head as far as is comfortable, then lower.

Then roll onto your side, drop your legs over the edge of the bed and push up with your arms to sit. Sit for a moment before standing. If morning stiffness is a big problem, our morning stretches tip has more ideas, and a warm shower before exercising often helps.

Part 2: 10-minute morning routine

Do this after breakfast or once you have been moving for a little while. You can do it standing, holding the back of a sturdy chair or the kitchen worktop, or sitting on a firm chair without arms.

MovementHow to do itReps
MarchingMarch on the spot, or lift your knees alternately while seated1 minute
Neck turnsSlowly turn your head to look over one shoulder, then the other5 each side
Neck tiltsGently tilt your ear towards your shoulder, each side5 each side
Shoulder rollsRoll your shoulders up, back and down in a circle10
Arm raisesRaise your arms forwards and up as far as is comfortable, then lower5 to 10
Trunk turnsArms crossed over your chest, turn your upper body gently to each side5 each side
Side bendsSlide one hand down the side of your leg, return, then the other side5 each side
Hip circles (standing)Hands on hips, gently circle your hips5 each way
Leg swings (standing, holding support)Gently swing one leg forwards and back, then swap5 to 10 each leg
Knee lifts or seated knee straighteningLift a knee towards your chest, or straighten a knee while seated5 to 10 each leg
Ankle circlesLift one foot and draw circles with your toes5 each way, each foot
Hand routineMake a gentle fist, open wide, touch each fingertip to your thumb5 each

Part 3: Movement snacks through the day

Stiffness often builds up when you sit or stand in one position. Aim to move for a minute or two every 30 to 60 minutes. Ideas:

  • At a desk: shoulder rolls, neck turns, wrist circles, seated marching, and standing up to walk to the kitchen.
  • Watching TV: during adverts or between episodes, do 10 ankle pumps, 5 knee straightens each leg and 5 sit-to-stands.
  • In the kitchen: while the kettle boils, do heel raises, side steps or gentle hip circles holding the worktop.
  • On a long journey: stop every hour or so to walk around, and do ankle pumps and shoulder rolls as a passenger.
  • Working on a computer or phone: stretch your fingers wide and do a few wrist bends every 30 minutes.

Setting a reminder on your phone or watch can help these become a habit.

Part 4: Evening wind-down (5 to 10 minutes)

Gentle movement and stretching in the evening can ease the stiffness of the day and help you relax before bed.

  1. Gentle walk around the house, 2 minutes.
  2. Calf stretch. Hands on a wall, one foot back, heel down, lean forward until you feel a stretch. Hold 20 to 30 seconds each side.
  3. Thigh stretch (seated). Sit near the edge of a chair, put one leg straight out with the heel on the floor and lean forward gently from the hips. Hold 20 to 30 seconds each side.
  4. Chest stretch. Clasp your hands behind your back, or hold your arms out to the sides, and gently open your chest. Hold 20 to 30 seconds.
  5. Knee to chest (lying on the bed). Hug one knee gently towards your chest. Hold 20 seconds each side.
  6. Relaxed breathing. Five slow breaths, letting your shoulders drop as you breathe out.

For joint-specific stretches, see our guides such as stretching for knee arthritis.

Swaps for different joints and abilities

If you haveTryGo easy on
Knee arthritisHeel slides, seated knee straightening, cyclingDeep knee bends, kneeling
Hip arthritisKnee rocking, gentle hip circles, leg swings holding supportForcing hips into deep bending or wide positions
Hand arthritisFinger opening, thumb touches, movements in warm waterTight fists if very painful, forcing fingers straight
Shoulder arthritisPendulum swings, supported arm raises, shoulder rollsFast or forced reaching overhead or behind your back
Back or neck arthritisPelvic tilts, knee rocking, gentle neck turnsFast twisting, looking up for long periods
Axial spondyloarthritisDaily spinal mobility and posture exercises; the NHS recommends regular exercise as an important part of treatmentLong periods of sitting without breaks
Balance problems or frailtySeated versions of all moves; see our chair exercise guideStanding exercises without support

If you have had a joint replacement, follow any movement precautions your surgical team or physiotherapist has given you.

On flare days

Keep doing gentle mobility on flare days if you can, but reduce the number of repetitions and skip movements that hurt the flaring joint. Gentle movement can help prevent the extra stiffness that rest brings. Our guide to exercise during a flare-up has a 10-minute flare-day routine.

Progressing your routine

  • Increase repetitions from 5 to 10, then do two rounds.
  • Gradually increase the range of movement, within comfort.
  • Move from seated to standing versions, holding support.
  • Add a strengthening session two days a week and build up your walking or other aerobic activity.
  • Try a class such as tai chi, gentle yoga or Pilates, which include mobility work.

Keep track of your stiffness

A simple record helps you see whether your routine is working. Each morning, note roughly how long your stiffness lasts and score it from 0 to 10. Once a week, check something practical, such as how easily you can put on your socks, look over your shoulder or reach a high cupboard. Many people notice they loosen up more quickly within a few weeks of daily mobility. If stiffness is getting worse despite a regular routine, mention it to your GP or physiotherapist.

Making it stick

  • Link it to something you already do. Do the bed routine before you get up, the morning routine after breakfast, and the evening routine before brushing your teeth.
  • Keep it visible. Write the routine on a card and keep it by the bed or on the fridge.
  • Start small. Even 2 minutes counts. You can add more once the habit is formed.
  • Do it with someone. A partner, friend or family member can join in, or you could join a gentle class.
  • Use music. A favourite song lasts about 3 to 4 minutes, enough for several movements.

Useful equipment (optional)

You do not need any equipment, but some people find these helpful: a sturdy chair without arms, a non-slip mat, a rolled towel to support your neck or knees when lying down, and a bowl of warm water for hand movements. A long-handled shoe horn or sock aid can make dressing easier while you work on hip and back mobility.

A simple weekly plan

Every day2 to 3 days a weekMost days
Bed wake-up, morning routine, movement snacks, evening wind-downStrength exercisesWalking, cycling, swimming or other aerobic activity, building towards 150 minutes a week

When to get medical help

  • Call NHS 111 or go to A&E if a joint suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially with a high temperature.
  • See your GP if you have morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes most days with swollen joints, as this can be a sign of inflammatory arthritis that needs assessing. Also see your GP if stiffness is getting steadily worse.
  • See a physiotherapist (via your GP or self-referral where available) if you are losing movement in a joint, or if mobility exercises consistently make your pain worse.
  • Stop and get urgent help if you feel dizzy, have chest pain or become very short of breath while exercising.

How often should I do mobility exercises?

Every day is ideal. Short sessions several times a day, such as in the morning, during the day and in the evening, are often more effective for stiffness than one long session.

Should I do mobility exercises if they hurt?

Mild discomfort or stretching is fine. Sharp pain, or pain that lasts more than a day, means you should reduce the range or repetitions. If movements keep causing pain, ask a physiotherapist to check your routine.

What is the best time of day for mobility exercises?

Many people find a short routine in the morning helps with stiffness, and an evening routine helps them wind down. Do what fits your day; consistency matters more than timing.

Can mobility exercises reduce morning stiffness?

Many people find gentle movement in bed and a short routine after getting up eases morning stiffness. A warm shower before moving can also help.

Is a mobility routine enough exercise for arthritis?

Mobility is a helpful part of your routine, but it is not enough on its own. NICE recommends muscle strengthening and aerobic exercise for osteoarthritis, so aim to include both alongside daily mobility.

Can I do mobility exercises sitting down?

Yes. Almost every movement in this routine can be done sitting on a firm chair. Seated versions are a good choice if you have balance problems or painful legs.
